clue.text: Shot during surrender

parts.note: a shot is a go or attempt, as is a turn
in means during, as in 'in the night'

explanation.surface: A soldier fires a shot in the middle of laying down arms.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn in is a phrasal verb for handing yourself or something over to the authorities, giving it up.

clue.text: Occasions for millions to stuff restrictions

indicators.note: to stuff means the millions are packed inside the restrictions

parts.note: ties are restrictions or bonds

explanation.surface: Times when vast sums are used to fill out regulations.
explanation.definitionFit: Times are occasions or instances, as in 'three times'.

clue.text: Free from obligation with regard to rental agreement

parts.note: re means with regard to
a lease is a rental contract

explanation.surface: A tenant is let off duties under a tenancy contract.
explanation.definitionFit: To release someone is to let them off a duty or contract, setting them at liberty.

clue.text: Meddle with current rent-free arrangement

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current in physics

indicators.note: arrangement means the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stirs up trouble with a living set-up where nobody pays rent.
explanation.definitionFit: To interfere is to intrude in others' affairs, the same sense as poking your nose in.

clue.text: Time to track back in great numbers

indicators.note: back tells us the word for the track is read from its end to its start

parts.note: a spoor is the track or trail of an animal

explanation.surface: An instruction to retrace one's path while surrounded by crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SPOOR, an animal's trail, into ROOPS; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops can mean large crowds or bodies of people, not just soldiers, so the plural noun fits a crowd sense.

clue.text: Complain — not great at first in stir

indicators.note: not means that letter is left out of the word for complain

parts.note: to grouse is to complain

indicators.note: at first picks the opening letter of great

parts.note: the opening letter of great

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that a stay in prison was not great at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stir' is British slang for prison, which is the surface reading; here it is the verb to wake or provoke.
explanation.definitionFit: To rouse is to wake or stir someone into activity.

clue.text: Best to beat it? Heading north after work

indicators.note: after places the reversed letters behind the work

parts.note: op is short for opus, a musical work

indicators.note: heading north in a down entry means the letters are read upwards, in reverse

parts.note: to lam is slang for to beat or thrash

explanation.surface: Advice that the best way to escape is to head north once the job is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat it' looks like slang for running away, but 'beat' is LAM and 'it' is IT, and 'Heading north' turns LAMIT into TIMAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Optimal means the most favourable or ideal, the top choice.

clue.text: Was suspicious of fish-eating American animal getting upset

indicators.note: eating puts the reversed letters inside the fish

parts.note: a smelt is a small fish

indicators.note: upset in a down entry means turned upside down, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: a rat is an animal

explanation.surface: A fish-eating creature from America gets agitated.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'fish-eating' glues the words into one adjective; split them, and the fish is doing the eating.
explanation.definitionFit: To smell a rat is an idiom for sensing that something is wrong, being suspicious.

clue.text: Former pupil reflective, during summer, in Paris Match

indicators.note: during places the reversed former pupil inside the French summer

parts.note: été is French for summer, written without its accents

indicators.note: reflective suggests a mirror image, so the word for former pupil is read backwards

parts.note: an alum is a former pupil or graduate (short for alumnus)

explanation.surface: A thoughtful ex-student reading Paris Match magazine while on a summer holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris Match is a French magazine, which disguises 'Match' as part of a title; 'in Paris' tells you to use the French word for summer.
explanation.definitionFit: To match someone is to equal or copy their achievement, which is what imitating or rivalling them amounts to.

clue.text: More cat hair mostly in that place

parts.note: a cat's hair is its fur

indicators.note: mostly means the word is used with its last letter left off

parts.note: there means in that place

explanation.surface: Someone finds yet more cat hair over there, on the sofa perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Further as an adjective means additional, extra, as in 'further details'.

clue.text: Sooty to identify dangerous place

parts.note: sooty means black, covered in soot
to spot is to identify or notice

explanation.surface: Sooty, the British children's TV glove puppet bear, is pointing out a hazard.
explanation.definitionFit: A black spot is a stretch of road with many accidents, a hazard zone.

clue.text: Lad with pliers repaired Earl's shoe

indicators.note: repaired suggests the letters are fixed and put back together in a new order

parts.note: E is a common abbreviation for Earl, as in the peerage

explanation.surface: A boy with a pair of pliers mends an aristocrat's shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: An espadrille is a light canvas shoe with a rope sole, a kind of summer footwear.

clue.text: Fellow worker's mother runs off

indicators.note: off says the runs are taken away from the word for mother

parts.note: mater is Latin for mother, still used jokingly in Britain
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A colleague's mum leaves in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A mate is a workmate or assistant, as in a plumber's mate who works alongside a tradesman.

clue.text: Public display of anger witnessed on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard rather than seen, so the word is taken as it sounds

parts.note: witnessed means seen

explanation.surface: A furious outburst heard by listeners of a radio broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Making a scene is an idiom for a loud emotional row in public.

clue.text: Draw from opening of spy story by ship's officer

indicators.note: opening of picks the first letter of spy

parts.note: the opening letter of spy
a tale is a story
a mate is a deck officer on a merchant ship

explanation.surface: A spy novel's opening lines, written by a sailor, are drawn on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draw' as the result of a game, not a sketch.
explanation.definitionFit: Stalemate in chess is a position with no legal move, ending the game as a draw.

clue.text: Chum's swallowing Labour leader's nonsense

indicators.note: swallowing puts the leader's letter inside the friends' word

parts.note: cobber is Australian slang for a friend; the plural reading gives cobbers

indicators.note: leader means the front letter of the word Labour is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Labour

explanation.surface: A political pal is taking in what the Labour Party leader says, and it is nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: Cobber is Australian slang for a mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobblers is British slang for rubbish talk, from rhyming slang, and means the same as drivel.

clue.text: Support for old club starts to reinvigorate Everton

parts.note: a brassie is an old name for a golf club, the two-wood

indicators.note: starts to picks the first letters of the two words that follow

parts.note: the first letter of reinvigorate
the first letter of Everton

explanation.surface: Backing from a historic football club to revive Everton, a Liverpool football team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old club' suggests a football club, but it is a golf club, the brassie.
explanation.definitionFit: A brassiere is a bra, an undergarment giving bust support.

clue.text: Organ grinder finally tucking into assorted canapés

indicators.note: tucking into, like eating, puts the letter inside the jumbled snacks
assorted canapés are a mixed selection, so the letters are jumbled
finally picks the closing letter of grinder

parts.note: the closing letter of grinder

explanation.surface: An organ grinder at a party eating a plate of mixed snacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organ grinder' is a set phrase, but 'Organ' is the definition and 'grinder' only gives its last letter R. 'assorted' turns CANAPES into PANCEAS, and the R goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The pancreas is a gland in the abdomen, a body organ producing insulin and digestive juices.

clue.text: Politician dispatched by agreement

parts.note: a Con is a Conservative politician
sent means dispatched

explanation.surface: A politician sent away by mutual accord.
explanation.definitionFit: Consent is permission or assent to something proposed.

clue.text: Bringer of good luck needing no introduction in town

indicators.note: no introduction means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a mascot is a person or thing thought to bring luck

explanation.surface: A lucky charm so famous in a town that nobody needs to introduce it.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a town in Berkshire, England, famous for its racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is an English town in Berkshire, home of the Royal Ascot race meeting.

clue.text: Those colluding may be in them?

definitions.text: Those colluding may be in them?

parts.words: Those colluding may be in them
parts.note: people plotting together are said to be 'in' this, an idiom for secret partnership; the clue describes the word by its set phrase

explanation.walkthrough: The clue points to the fixed phrase about conspirators being 'in' something together.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in cahoots is an idiom for secret partnership with someone, usually to do something dishonest.

clue.text: Contents of file? Another list

indicators.note: contents of says the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone asks what's in a file, then offers another list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'list' looks like a noun after 'Another', but it is the verb meaning to tilt, as a ship lists.
explanation.definitionFit: To list is to tilt to one side, as a ship does, which is what leaning means.

clue.text: The largest part of ship filled with animals? Just the opposite

indicators.note: filled with would put the animals inside the ship
just the opposite reverses that, so the ship goes inside the animals instead

parts.note: a lion and a hare are both animals
SS is the abbreviation for steamship

explanation.surface: A cargo ship mostly filled with livestock, like Noah's ark.
explanation.walkthrough: Read at face value the ship holds the animals; 'Just the opposite' turns the container round, so the animals hold the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The lion's share is an idiom for the biggest portion, from Aesop's fable where the lion takes everything.

clue.text: Person avoiding company of fellow beyond help has left for good

indicators.note: has left for good means left takes the place of good

parts.note: a goner is someone beyond saving

explanation.surface: A recluse dies having left for ever, abandoning a hopeless friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has left for good' reads as gone for ever; here L replaces G.
explanation.definitionFit: A loner is someone who prefers solitude, keeping away from other people.

clue.text: Argument at home over sharing work

indicators.note: over in a down entry means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: to run means to work or operate, as an engine runs
in means at home

explanation.surface: A domestic row about dividing up the chores.
explanation.definitionFit: A run-in is an informal word for a quarrel or confrontation, often with authority.

clue.text: Attendant largely opposed to showy display

parts.note: a page is a young attendant, at a wedding or court

indicators.note: largely means most of the word, its last letter dropped

parts.note: anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: A court attendant who mostly dislikes ostentatious displays.
explanation.definitionFit: A pageant is an elaborate public show or procession, often in costume, put on for spectacle.

clue.text: Perhaps Joan of Arc's horse gets home at last

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin

indicators.note: at last picks the closing letter of home

parts.note: the last letter of home

explanation.surface: Joan of Arc's warhorse finally makes it back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horse' looks like Joan's steed, but it is drug slang for heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan of Arc is an example of a celebrated woman of courage, a female hero of French history.

clue.text: Screw former revolutionary on the way back

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: on the way back means the word for the revolutionary is read in reverse

parts.note: a Trot is short for a Trotskyist, a revolutionary

explanation.surface: A one-time revolutionary squeezes someone while heading home.
explanation.definitionFit: To screw money out of someone is slang for extracting it by force or threats.

clue.text: Argue about crime Morse essentially dismissed

parts.note: re means about, concerning

indicators.note: dismissed means that central letter is sent away from the crime

parts.note: arson is the crime of setting fire to property

indicators.note: essentially means at its heart, the central letter of Morse

parts.note: the central letter of Morse

explanation.surface: A debate about a crime that Inspector Morse has dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a British TV detective, which makes 'crime' look like a case. 'essentially' gives R, the middle of MORSE, and 'dismissed' removes it from ARSON to leave ASON.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason with someone is to argue or present a logical case to persuade them.
